tips.body: Transition metals are **higher** in melting point, density, strength and hardness — and **lower** in reactivity. Remembering *they are better* gets the reactivity wrong, and lower reactivity is what makes them useful.

steps.title: Where they are, and what this covers
steps.body:
**This topic is chemistry only.** It is not on the combined science course.

The **transition elements** are the block of metals in the middle of the periodic table, between Group 2 and Group 3.

**The specification's definition is a comparison:**

> **The transition elements are metals with similar properties which are different from those of the elements in Group 1.**

So the whole topic is set up as a contrast with Group 1, and every question about it is really asking *how are these different from the alkali metals?*

**The six elements to use as examples** are named by the spec, and you should use them rather than inventing others:

**chromium (Cr), manganese (Mn), iron (Fe), cobalt (Co), nickel (Ni), copper (Cu)**

These are the ones the examiners have in mind, and their compounds are the ones whose colours you are expected to know.

**Two spec points, two halves of the topic:**

1. **Comparison with Group 1** — melting points, densities, strength, hardness, and reactivity.
2. **Typical properties** — ions with different charges, coloured compounds, and use as catalysts.

Knowing that it splits in two is useful, because a question will usually be about one half or the other.

steps.title: Compared with Group 1
steps.body:
The spec asks you to **describe the difference compared with Group 1** on **five** things. All five, and four of them run the same way while one runs the other.

**Transition metals have:**

- **higher melting points** — iron melts at over 1500 °C; sodium at 98 °C
- **higher densities** — Group 1 metals are so light that lithium, sodium and potassium **float on water**
- **greater strength**
- **greater hardness** — Group 1 metals can be **cut with a knife**

**But lower reactivity** with **oxygen, water and halogens** — and this is the one that runs the other way.

**The reactivity difference is the most striking.** Put sodium in water and it reacts violently, melting into a ball and racing about. Put iron in water and it does **nothing** you can see — it rusts, slowly, over months, and only in the presence of **both** water and oxygen.

**Why this matters practically.** Transition metals are the metals we **build with**: strong, hard, high-melting, and unreactive enough to last. Group 1 metals are stored **under oil**, because they would otherwise react with the air. You could not make a bridge out of sodium, and the reason is every item in this list at once.

**A caution.** The comparison is with **Group 1**, not with metals in general. And *higher melting point* is a comparison, not an absolute — mercury is a transition metal and is **liquid** at room temperature. Questions are set on the general comparison, but knowing the exception shows judgement.

steps.title: Typical properties
steps.body:
**Many transition elements have ions with different charges, form coloured compounds, and are useful as catalysts.**

That single sentence is the second spec point, and all three parts are examinable.

**1. Ions with different charges.** A Group 1 metal forms only a **1+** ion — it has one outer electron and that is that. A transition metal can form **more than one** ion:

- **iron** forms $\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}$ and $\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}$
- **copper** forms $\mathrm{Cu^{+}}$ and $\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}$

This is why compounds are named with a **Roman numeral**: **iron(II) chloride** and **iron(III) chloride** are different compounds, and the numeral says which ion is present. If a question gives you *copper(II) sulfate*, the **(II)** is telling you the charge.

**2. Coloured compounds.** Group 1 compounds are almost all **white**, and dissolve to give **colourless** solutions. Transition metal compounds are **coloured**, and the colour depends on the metal **and** on its charge:

- **copper(II)** compounds are **blue**
- **iron(II)** compounds are **green**
- **iron(III)** compounds are **brown**

Those three you should know, because they are exactly the colours used in the **metal hydroxide tests**. This topic and the ion tests are the same facts seen twice.

**3. Useful as catalysts.** A **catalyst** speeds up a reaction without being used up. Transition metals and their compounds are unusually good at it:

- **iron** in the **Haber process**, making ammonia
- **nickel** in the **hydrogenation** of alkenes, hardening vegetable oils
- **manganese(IV) oxide** in the decomposition of **hydrogen peroxide**

**All three properties can be exemplified by Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, Ni and Cu** — the spec's own list, and the one to draw examples from.

steps.title: Your turn
steps.body:
**Part A.**

1. Name the six elements the specification uses as examples of transition metals.
2. Give three ways transition metals differ from Group 1 metals.
3. Name the three typical properties of transition metals.

**Part B.**

4. Why is copper sulfate written as copper(II) sulfate?
5. Give the colours of copper(II), iron(II) and iron(III) compounds.
6. Give two examples of a transition metal used as a catalyst, and say what reaction each catalyses.

**Part C.**

7. Explain why transition metals are used to build bridges and Group 1 metals are not, referring to at least three properties.
8. A white solid dissolves to give a colourless solution. Is it more likely to be a Group 1 compound or a transition metal compound? Explain.
9. Explain why Group 1 metals do not need a Roman numeral in their names but transition metals usually do.

For question 2, the spec names **five** points of comparison, and one of them runs the opposite way to the rest.

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**Four properties one way, one the other.** Transition metals are **higher** in melting point, density, strength and hardness, and **lower** in reactivity. A student who remembers *transition metals are better* will get the reactivity wrong, because lower reactivity is what makes them useful — not a shortcoming.

**The five comparisons are named in the spec**, so a question asking you to compare transition metals with Group 1 has five available lines. Giving three answers three fifths of it.

**The Roman numeral is information, not decoration.** It exists **because the charge is not fixed**. Group 1 metals always form 1+ ions, so *sodium chloride* is unambiguous. Copper forms $\mathrm{Cu^{+}}$ and $\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}$, so *copper chloride* would not say which compound is meant. Whenever you see a numeral, the question has handed you the **charge** — which you need for writing the formula.

**Colour is a diagnostic, and you already use it.** Copper(II) **blue**, iron(II) **green**, iron(III) **brown** are the same three colours that identify those ions in the **sodium hydroxide precipitate test**. The two topics are one set of facts approached from different directions, and noticing that halves what there is to learn.

**Why they make good catalysts** is not required, but it follows from the first property: because a transition metal can exist in **more than one oxidation state**, it can accept electrons at one stage of a reaction and give them back at another, providing a path of lower activation energy and emerging unchanged. That connects all three typical properties to the same underlying cause.

**Mercury is the exception worth knowing.** It is a transition metal and it is **liquid** at room temperature. The general comparison with Group 1 still holds, and noting the exception shows you are describing a **trend** rather than reciting a rule.

**The practical point ties it together.** Transition metals are the metals we **build** with — strong, hard, high-melting and unreactive enough to survive. Group 1 metals are kept **under oil** so they do not react with the air. Every property in this topic shows up in that one contrast.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- This topic is **chemistry only**.
- **Transition elements are metals with similar properties which are different from those of Group 1.**
- The six examples the spec names: **Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, Ni, Cu**.
- Compared with **Group 1**, transition metals have **higher melting points**, **higher densities**, **greater strength** and **greater hardness**.
- But they are **less reactive** with **oxygen, water and halogens** — the one comparison that runs the other way.
- Group 1 metals are **soft enough to cut with a knife**, **float on water**, and are stored **under oil**.
- **Many transition elements have ions with different charges**: $\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}$ and $\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}$, $\mathrm{Cu^{+}}$ and $\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}$.
- That is why names carry a **Roman numeral** — it gives the **charge**.
- **They form coloured compounds**: copper(II) **blue**, iron(II) **green**, iron(III) **brown**.
- Group 1 compounds are almost all **white**, giving **colourless** solutions.
- **They are useful as catalysts**: **iron** in the **Haber process**, **nickel** in **hydrogenation**, **manganese(IV) oxide** with **hydrogen peroxide**.
- The compound colours are the **same three** used in the metal hydroxide tests.
- **Mercury** is a transition metal that is **liquid** at room temperature.

questions.prompt: Compare transition metals with the elements of Group 1, referring to all the properties named in the specification.
questions.solution: Transition metals are the block of metals in the centre of the periodic table, and although they are metals like the elements of Group 1 their properties are markedly different. In terms of melting point, transition metals melt at much higher temperatures, with iron melting above fifteen hundred degrees Celsius whereas sodium melts at only ninety eight degrees. They also have much higher densities, which is why lithium, sodium and potassium are light enough to float on water while a transition metal sinks. Transition metals are considerably stronger and also much harder, whereas Group 1 metals are soft enough to be cut with a knife. On all four of these properties the transition metals are the higher, but the fifth comparison runs the other way. Transition metals are much less reactive than Group 1 metals with oxygen, water and halogens. Sodium reacts violently with water, melting into a ball and moving rapidly across the surface, while iron shows no visible reaction with water at all and rusts only slowly and only when both water and oxygen are present. Group 1 metals must therefore be stored under oil to keep them from reacting with the air, which transition metals do not require. Taken together these differences explain why transition metals are the metals used for construction, since they are strong, hard, high melting and unreactive enough to last, while no structure could be built from a Group 1 metal. It is worth noting that mercury is an exception among transition metals in being liquid at room temperature.

questions.modelAnswer:
**The five comparisons the specification names — four run one way, one the other:**

| Property | Transition metals | Group 1 |
|---|---|---|
| melting points | **higher** — iron above 1500 °C | low — sodium at 98 °C |
| densities | **higher** | low — they **float on water** |
| strength | **greater** | weak |
| hardness | **harder** | **cut with a knife** |
| reactivity | **lower** | very high — **stored under oil** |

**The reactivity difference, shown:** sodium in water reacts violently, melting into a ball and racing about. Iron in water does **nothing visible** — it rusts slowly, and only with **both** water and oxygen present.

**The conclusion that ties it together:** transition metals are the metals we **build** with, because they are strong, hard, high-melting and unreactive enough to last. No structure could be made from a Group 1 metal.

**And the exception worth knowing:** **mercury** is a transition metal that is **liquid** at room temperature — which shows you are describing a trend rather than reciting a rule.

questions.prompt: Describe the three typical properties of transition metals, and explain how they are connected.
questions.solution: Many transition elements have ions with different charges, form coloured compounds and are useful as catalysts. Taking these in turn, the first means that the same metal can form more than one ion, so iron forms both Fe two plus and Fe three plus and copper forms both Cu plus and Cu two plus. This is why the names of their compounds carry a Roman numeral, since copper sulfate alone would not say which ion is present, and copper two sulfate specifies the charge. The second property is that their compounds are coloured, unlike those of Group 1 which are almost all white and give colourless solutions. The colour depends on both the metal and its charge, so copper two compounds are blue, iron two compounds are green and iron three compounds are brown. These are the same three colours used to identify those ions in the sodium hydroxide precipitate test, so the two topics are a single set of facts approached from different directions. The third property is that transition metals and their compounds are widely used as catalysts, substances which speed up a reaction without being used up, with iron used in the Haber process and nickel in the hydrogenation of alkenes. The three properties are connected because they all follow from the ability of a transition metal to exist in more than one oxidation state. That ability is the first property directly, it affects the colour of the compound formed, which is the second, and it allows the metal to accept electrons at one stage of a reaction and return them at another, providing a lower energy route and emerging unchanged, which is the third.

questions.modelAnswer:
**The three properties**, from the spec's own sentence: transition elements have **ions with different charges**, form **coloured compounds**, and are **useful as catalysts**.

**1. Different charges.** Iron forms $\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}$ and $\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}$; copper forms $\mathrm{Cu^{+}}$ and $\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}$. This is why names carry a **Roman numeral** — *copper sulfate* alone would be ambiguous, and *copper(II) sulfate* gives the charge.

**2. Coloured compounds.** Unlike Group 1's white solids and colourless solutions. **Copper(II) blue, iron(II) green, iron(III) brown** — the same three colours as the **sodium hydroxide precipitate tests**, so the two topics are one set of facts seen twice.

**3. Catalysts.** **Iron** in the Haber process; **nickel** in hydrogenation.

**How they connect — and this is the mark that lifts the answer.** All three follow from the ability to exist in **more than one oxidation state**:

- that ability **is** the first property;
- it **affects the colour** of the compound, giving the second;
- and it lets the metal **accept electrons at one stage and return them at another**, providing a lower-energy route and emerging unchanged — which is the third.

examTechnique.body:
Compare with Group 1 on all five properties the specification names.

Remember that reactivity is the comparison that runs the other way: transition metals are less reactive.

Draw examples from Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, Ni and Cu.

Read a Roman numeral as the charge on the ion.

Give the compound colours as copper(II) blue, iron(II) green and iron(III) brown.

Name a catalyst together with the reaction it catalyses.

Use the absence of colour as evidence for a Group 1 compound.

Remember this content is chemistry only.
examinerErrors: Saying transition metals are more reactive than Group 1 metals.
Comparing on only two or three properties when five are named.
Treating the Roman numeral as part of the name with no meaning.
Naming a catalyst without saying what it catalyses.
Giving the wrong colour for iron(II) or iron(III).
Claiming all transition metals are solid, forgetting mercury.
Using elements outside the specification's list as examples.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer knows the comparison with Group 1 is five-sided and that reactivity is the one that inverts, and it treats lower reactivity as the reason transition metals are useful rather than as a weakness. It reads a Roman numeral as the charge on the ion and knows why Group 1 names need none. It recognises that the compound colours are the ion-test colours, and it can connect all three typical properties to a single cause: the ability to exist in more than one oxidation state.
